chapter: Radio color line, San Francisco and Columbia staff
title: Studying timpani and teaching himself xylophone
summary: Lee studied timpani with Mr. White and taught himself xylophone because studio drummers had to be more than traps players.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: vibes, and I studied timpanies from a man -- he was Professor White; he was about -- he was here in Los Angeles, he worked the studios, but maybe I jumped some of the things.

I believe that you have to be prepared for whatever is to come, you know? And when I was telling you when I started freelancing at the studios, then I also started studying, because when you work at the studios, I saw what the other drummers had to do, and I didn't want to be one dimensional.

Now they hired me at these studios because the drummers at the time, that they had, they were legit drummers, you know, they couldn't really play time, so what I was called for was to play what they called the 'traps' -- you know? Play the snare, the bass drum and all of that. But these other fellows, they could roll on their drums and sound like tissue paper tearing, you know, because they were really legit -- they could play all the mallot instruments; they played the marimbas and the chimes and the bells, and then I studied timpany from a man called Mr. White who worked at -- he worked at Fox studios.
Do you remember Mr. White's first name?

I can't remember it. I don't know why I want to say Charlie, but I don't know -- I'm not sure what it was. But anyway, -- and then the xylophones I taught myself, because I bought them and took them home and put them up in Lee's room, and I used to practice 3 or 4 hours a day. And

that's not hard to teach, you know, the methods. You're already a musician, and I already knew the keyboard to the piano, and you get the method and then what you have to do is practice running scales and practice reading. It's not that hard once you've been in to it.
So I worked at Columbia ... date
